He said: Madam Speaker, the reason that I moved this motion on behalf of my colleague for Scarborough- Rouge River and members of the Liberal caucus is that the whole question of noise abatement and noise pollution with regard to communities that abut major international airports like the one at Pearson International Airport in metropolitan Toronto is a very serious one.
It is also a very responsible one. You do not hear these communities suggesting that somehow Pearson International Airport is going to shut down or that we are going to go back to the horse drawn cart rather than have the noise of modem aircraft.
Whether you live by an airport or very far from an airport you obviously understand that air travel is not only here to stay but is on the increase because life is increasingly in the fast lane despite the fact that the numbers of travellers are down because of the economic recession and the problems that the airlines face as a result.
Therefore, the purpose of Bill C-5 is to try to come to grips with controlling and managing this because there needs to be a recognition of the vitality of any airport, the multiplier effect that an airport clearly brings to metropolitan Toronto, Montreal or Vancouver, and the needs of a Canadian domestic and international travelling public. We need to balance all those factors with the need for communities to be communities, to allow those neighbourhoods to continue rather than forcing people to pick up and move because of the airport situation.
We have tried to put an amendment through today that speaks to the fact that airlines would be pleased to pay or chance the penalty for violating a noise regulation as part of doing business. It might be profitable for them to simply absorb the penalty or try to appeal the situation because there are many more fines levied than there are actual fines paid.
It was brought to our attention by officials of the Department of Transport that some of the more flagrant abusers are foreign air carriers coming to and going from

Government Orders
Pearson International Airport and other airports across the country.
My amendment would suggest that we try to stop and disallow any pattern of behaviour by any airline that wishes to pay the penalty costs regularly as part of doing business at Canadian international airports and therefore run roughshod over the regulations we have to protect the surrounding communities. Specifically my amendment would suggest that on the third noise violation by that one airline, it become mandatory for the minister and the department and indeed the government to simply remove that aviation document from that airline. This would effectively preclude that airline from doing business at that airport in Canada.
We feel that this would be in fact some tough medicine and would send out a very direct and clear message to particularly the foreign aircraft carriers whose regulations may differ with those they may find in Canada. The message is that we want to respect the balance between the vitality of an airport and the vitality of the communities which surround that airport. The minister has the option now to withdraw that document. It is not a mandatory one. It is an optional one.
What we would like to do is simply crystallize that, make it mandatory and begin to discourage any airline from thinking that rather than complying with our noise regulations and our time curfews, it should go ahead, pay the penalty and take a chance because it has a full load and some money in the bank anyway.
What my amendment does is to go beyond simply the minister or the government having the option to exercise some toughness. Obviously there are some special powers that all ministers have over their departments in very special or emergency cases. But we would like to make it part of the new stricter noise regulations that will be flowing from Bill C-5 if it becomes legislation. We would like to take it one step further and remove the potential systematic abuse of noise regulations by airlines which is to the detriment of surrounding communities. According to the evidence of the department this particularly concerns foreign aircraft.

Madam Speaker, I rise in support of my colleague's amendment. Veiy briefly, I just want to point out that as he has
already said the monetary fines tend to be more like a licence fee.
We have given the judiciary the power to impose fees of up to $25,000 because of an amendment that was accepted by all parties in committee. I think looking at the record we whl find that there were 2,599 complaints received between April 1, 1988 to March 31, 1989. Of these, 1,783 were handled administratively, 78 by judicial action and 738 were concluded with no investigation conducted.
Administrative monetary penalties were assessed in 347 counts with the average penalty being $215. Fines were imposed in 157 counts heard in court. The average fine per count amounted to $314.
In the initial case, $215 is considerably less than the price of almost any ticket flying into Tbronto, Mirabel or Dorval. Three hundred and fourteen dollars maybe will be around the cost of a one way ticket flying into or out of any of those three airports. Even where we see a number of $500 fines imposed-this seems to be the more popular number-it costs me more than that to fly from Thunder Bay to Toronto to Ottawa and return.
Clearly the monetary fines that have been applied, even though the ceiling is nowhere near the amount of the fines, have not been sufficiently strong enough to convince the airlines to change their ways.
I think my colleague's amendment is a good move. It would make it mandatory to pull the ticket of an offending airline after it has offended the noise violations on three separate occasions.
The amendment does not say pull the ticket for life. It is not shutting down the airline. The government has the authority to do this now should it wish but it has not. If a ticket is pulled for a day or two I do not think there would be any problem whatsoever down the road.
I believe the airlines would think twice. Whether they are domestic carriers, those that survive, or whether they are international carriers coming into Canada, I believe they would think twice. This would be much the same way I might suggest that the zero tolerance laws regarding drugs allows governments to seize aircraft that have been found carrying drugs or illegal immigrants or what have you into various countries. That quickly puts a stop to that kind of illegal activity.
December 6, 1991

I would therefore encourage the government to give careful consideration to this power that parliamentarians want to give them so that they can show that they are prepared to get tough with noise polluters at Pearson International Airport, at Mirabel, at Vancouver, at Thunder Bay or at any of the airports where it has been a problem.

With respect to this particular amendment, my hon. colleague from Thunder Bay-Atikokan was just mentioning the fines that had been paid and how low they were. Of course this was done because the current threshold is only $1,000 as a maximum.
Under the new legislation, as was pointed out, the fines are going to go up to $25,000. The ability will be there to make them much more of a penalty than what they are today.
The minister now does have the authority to pull the ticket if that is the action that needs to be taken. We feel that leaving it as it is and not putting a three-flight or three-occasion clause in there gives us the ability to do it on the first offence if we find it so necessary. We would prefer to leave it that way.

She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to address the provisions of Bill C-5, an act to amend the Aeronautics Act and to amend an act to amend the Aeronautics Act.
At the outset I would like to extend my sincere thanks to the chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport and all the committee members for their diligence shown throughout the sittings and for their proposals to amend this bill in response to the representations that were made to them.
Some of the proposed amendments can be summarized as follows. The maximum penalty for the breach of a designated provision such as noise abatement procedures will be increased both for corporations and for individuals. A new section will be added to authorize the Minister of Transport to make interim orders that will immediately implement urgent safety recommendations received from bodies such as the Transportation Safety Board of Canada. In addition, the Minister of Transport will be given the power to withhold, suspend or cancel a Canadian aviation document when of the opinion that the document holder's past record justifies that action. This closes a loophole that existed in the previous legislation.
Another amendment to the original bill was unanimously agreed to by the members of the committee after representations from several concerned groups. This was ably proposed by my hon. friend opposite, the member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan. This amendment will add a new regulatory authority to the Aeronautics Act to set out the hours of work of crew members, including flight attendants. This move goes some way toward recognizing the important safety functions performed by flight attendants on commercial flights.
Other amendments will correct and update existing provisions in the Aeronautics Act.
The passage of this legislation has been eagerly awaited by the residents living near Canada's major airports, particularly the neighbours of Lester B. Pearson International Airport. In fact, the section of the legislation pertaining to increased fines for noise abatement or flight track infractions stems from extensive consultations with Pearson's neighbours. Municipal leaders and community groups told our officials that a

Government Orders
maximum fine of $1,000 was not enough by way of deterrent and we have listened to them.
This bill, as amended, now calls for a maximum fine of $25,000 for corporations and $5,000 for individuals. The corporate ceiling recommended by the standing committee as moved by my colleague the member for St. Catharines is higher than the initial one proposed in Bill C-5. My officials at Pearson advise me that the subject of increased fines is a topic frequently raised at the public meetings that they hold regularly. But increased fines are only part of the solution. At Pearson the most advanced noise-monitoring and flight-tracking system in the world has been installed and is already providing important information. The system will be fully operational when the new air traffic control system is completed.
Pearson's noise management office will have an automatic link between 14 new noise monitors installed in neighbourhoods around the airport and the radar system that tracks aircraft flight paths. In the past we relied primarily on complaints of nearby residents. With the new system, any deviation from approved flight paths or failure to follow the noise abatement procedures will be readily apparent.
I trust that we have also allayed the concerns of those representing the interests of the general aviation field with respect to the transfer of certain zoning authority from federal jurisdiction to provincial jurisdiction.
Another issue that we are pleased with is the support of Canadian air carriers and the Airline Pilots Association for the proposed amendment respecting the making of interim orders to give immediate effect to any recommendation necessary for aviation safety or the safety of the public following an accident or an incident investigation.
One of the concerns raised at the standing committee was the wording and intent of certain amendments proposed in clauses 12 and 13. This is also the subject of the further amendments that were presented to us today and put on the Order Paper as we heard by the member for Scarborough-Rouge River.
It should first be understood that these particular subclauses in Bill C-5 are consequential amendments of what has been in the original Aeronautics Act since its
passage in 1985. In these particular clauses the last subclause provided for a shift in the evidentiary burden to the accused where the regulation allegedly violated has not been published in the Canada Gazette. These subclauses address the situation where the department has taken other steps to bring the regulations to the attention of the accused. My friend from Scarborough- Rouge River gave notice to the amendments to C-5 to delete these two subclauses.
The department has well established practices for communication with the aviation community on regulatory provisions that are legally exempted from the publication requirements of the Statutory Instruments Act. It is the aviation community, as a very specialized and identifiable public, to which these provisions apply and not to the general public.
The primary vehicle for these communications is the notice to airmen, or NOTAM, which is distributed regularly to all licensed pilots and operators and is also made available through air traffic services facilities. The law requires that pilots familiarize themselves with all information appropriate to their intended flights. This includes familiarising themselves with all relevant NO-TAMs.
If an accused has a special and unique reason to believe that longstanding government and industry practices which have support in law were not appropriate in the particular case, it is only reasonable that the accused explain what these are.
It is for these reasons that the subsections in question shift the evidentiary burden to the accused. This is in our view entirely appropriate. If evidence exists to demonstrate that reasonable steps were not taken in respect to the accused, he or she would be in the best position to show this and would accordingly be found not guilty of a regulatory violation.
In conclusion, I would once again like to thank the committee members and the associations that appeared before the committee for their very valuable contributions to Bill C-5. I am hopeful that all members of the House will offer their support for this bill as we continue our endeavours to enhance the already commendable level of aviation safety in Canada.
December 6, 1991

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of of the member for Hamilton West and all of my caucus, I am pleased to respond to third reading of Bill C-5.
Essentially it is a bill that has obtained a fair amount of support from all sides. The main feature as the minister noted is the question of increased fines for airlines that abuse our noise regulations. The fines have been increased substantially. That needs to be said. Previous to Bill C-5 the fines stood for both individuals and the major corporations at $1,000.
Through the work of the committee, in conjunction with consultations within the constituency, including community groups, fines for individual small operators were raised to $5,000 and fines for corporations were raised to $25,000.
It is hoped this will discourage airlines which continue and seek to abuse our regulations. It is important to major airports of this country, as it is to airports around the world, for us to strike a balance. We cannot simply close our eyes or plug our ears in the name of advancing the question of air travel in our country or the question of expanding airports or the question of the jobs that come from airports. The fact is airports are here to stay.
Air travel is increasingly becoming popular with more Canadians from coast to coast to coast. That is well understood by communities around the airports and communities not close to the airports. There needs to be a balance to the other aspirations that are also equally important: the families, businesses and residential communities that are located and operate adjacent to international airports.
It is simply unfair for us to respond to those individuals by saying: "If you do not like it and if it is too noisy, just move". That is a glib answer which solves nothing for anyone.
We have to ensure when we plan for our transportation infrastructures, including airports, that those communities have every right to be viable communities like the rest across the country and that those families have every right to enjoy their local parts without being drowned by the constant flights in metro Toronto eveiy 30 seconds. These people have every right to enjoy the aesthetics that are part of our neighbourhoods.
Government Orders
Let us face it, at the end of the working day as the pace of life quickens and as the pace of life becomes more hectic, going home is a moment that people relish. Our homes are our castles. Our homes, on average, are the biggest investments that Canadians will ever make during their working lives. It is more than simply a place to stay; it becomes an escape. It becomes an opportunity for one to go home with one's family, with one's children and relax and enjoy and be prepared and get ready to face the world the next morning. Therefore, we need to be cognizant of and sensitive to those very real and needed aspirations.
When we talk about communities in metropolitan Toronto, we are not only talking about a few small neighbourhoods. The member for Broadview-Greenwood will be seeking the floor in a few moments and is going to tell of his riding which is far east of the airport, but from which complaints are coming that the aircraft are coming in regularly along the Don Valley and causing problems there.
There are problems in the south end of my riding in North York. There are problems in Mississauga. There are problems in Etobicoke. There are problems in Brampton. Pearson International Airport is the flagship airport of our country and is a major player internationally and therefore, quite properly, attracts major clientele from around the globe.
We are not talking about an isolated pocket. We are not talking about being parochial. We are talking about a real live phenomenon which has frustrated many individuals in and around Pearson International Airport.
I believe that when we talk about expansion, when we talk about privatization and when we talk about runways, we also need to talk about and be cognizant of the situation that those neighbourhoods will have to put up with. That is the cost of increasing air travel in and out of Pearson airport.
The airport noise situation and the whole question of the increased fines toward airlines that break those regulations are the centrepieces of Bill C-5.
The minister mentioned that there are a number of applications, for instance, better clarifying the zoning procedures in and around airports for the purpose of the aeronautics bill. It is going to be interesting to see what we do with the new hotel at terminal 3 at Pearson, which is four-stories too tall for the safety of airport travel.

Government Orders
It was also suggested giving the minister, in terms of reacting to calamities that unfortunately befall us from time to time, a quicker response. Rather than waiting for the regulatory process to kick in, a minister on a two-year basis can issue an intermediate response. This is good because I think in times of emergencies and in times of tragedies it is reassuring for a public, a government or a minister to be able to have the tools and the wherewithal to react quickly and succinctly to not only rid ourselves of that problem in the future, but to re-establish confidence and safety among the travelling public.
The question of increased fines is but one factor in a multiplicity of factors that contribute to a complex equation in terms of noise abatement. I appreciate that the minister is here in the House. I put a number of different measures forward at report stage and during committee, amendments that were thought to be outside of the purview of the bill, but I wish to put them back on the agenda as we speak today.
I do not think we should simply forget about these ideas because I do not think we have licked the noise problems with just this one piece of legislation, notwithstanding the fact that it is an improvement in terms of the fines.
One amendment I put forward is a noise insulation program that has worked very well and very effectively in the Denver community. The problem there was becoming quite acute. The situation there was very similar to that of the residents in Mississauga and in my riding where the houses, doors and windows would rattle when aircraft were flying low.
The Denver airport, in conjunction with government officials, basically applied state of the art technology in terms of insulation against the rattling and also abating the noise penetrating these homes and buildings. It has established an insulation program which is an incentive for the local communities to take advantage of.
I read an article in terms of the success the Denver- Stapleton International Airport had. It allows for funding from the government of upward of $7,500. There is a meeting half way between government and community
in terms of increasing and adapting technological insulation programs in keeping with the challenges.
In this country in the past we have had incentives in insulation programs. I would suggest that it would not be too far fetched, particularly for communities abutting the major international airports, to take a look at the experiment in Denver and see if we can adapt it. If we could, it would be a win situation. It would be a win for the government which is bombarded constantly with noise problems from communities that have nowhere else to turn.
It would be a win situation for the resident who would be assisted in purchasing that new insulation because the government would come in with some financial assistance. It would also be a win situation for employment and some activity, particularly in the trade sector in and around airports like metropolitan Toronto. We could get some of these contractors working again.
It is a situation which we simply should not just read about in a magazine and forget about. If it works in Denver, and it has had some success and there is going to be some financial commitment, I think there would be rewards for the government in terms of the work related activity and noise reduction. I think the government should seek to take advantage of the situation.
It is a program I recommend to the government to at least consider and study to see if it is something we might be able to adapt to our situation. If the Americans can make it work in Denver then I think Canadians can make it work in Toronto, Vancouver or Montreal.
I also had an amendment at report stage. I thought it would be good to have in our books on a mandatory basis the situation that would preclude an airline from thinking that it can simply run roughshod over our noise regulations and simply charge it as a price of doing business. For some major airlines or individuals perhaps $25,000 or $10,000 is a huge sum, and I do not want to belittle that.
For major international corporations, American or others, travelling around the clock to every comer of the world, perhaps it is not as big a bottom line as it is for individuals. Therefore there have been occasions, according to answers provided to us in committee by officials of the Department of Transport, in which

airlines have taken the attitude of simply ignoring the fees or charges that would be levied against them for that violation and would simply charge it up as part of doing business, assuming they have a full load and are making a good profit which means they will simply take it off the top.
I was suggesting that if an airline committed three violations against our noise standards and regulations, it would trigger a loss of its travelling document, its right to operate in and around our Canadian airports.
I think that would provide some teeth and a signal to send to aircraft carriers, particularly to foreign carriers which are the bulk of them, as we were told at committee. It would show that we are not taking things lightly when talking about the important balance between airports and communities around those airports. Some of these carriers operate in countries where there are no environmental or noise standards, and we ought to have them respect the decisions that we have taken for our own citizenry and respect them in a way that we will not be having a flagrant systematic abuse of our laws.
The minister right now, without Bill C-5, can obviously remove one's document after the first violation. The minister made mention of that. There is a great difference between an option and a mandatory reaction to an action. I was hoping that the minister and the government might see fit, in order to strengthen the teeth that we have in order to get these foreign air carriers to comply with our standards, to make it mandatory. I am hoping that the minister and government are serious that if there are airlines that make it a practice to break our laws, we will be tough with them. The reality is that very few of the airlines that been fined have paid for those fines. The people who pay for that in the end are Canadians who live around those airports and have to put up with a lot of noise and air pollution which they feel is absolutely unfair.
Another issue that I put forward comes from consulting with communities in Brampton, Etobicoke, Mississauga and North York, for which I give them credit, and that is to use the moneys or part of the moneys that we will be getting from these fines and channel them back into the local communities in order to come up with better noise abatement procedures or to basically reinvest them in the fight against airport noise.
Government Orders
It was very similar to the efforts of our colleagues on this side of the House in terms of the many petitions that we are gathering, myself included, and in terms of the confiscation of drugs. Not all those moneys go back to general revenues in Ottawa where you never see them again, but they somehow find themselves rechannelled back to the local police and the local organizations responsible for the real fight against drugs.
Taking a page from that book, we are advocating that if we are going to increase the fines levied against the airlines, and if we are serious about having those airlines pay those fines, it would be a novel idea to somehow, with proper accountability, use some of those moneys that have come from noise violators to advance the cause for a better system at the airport to monitor and to fight those noise violations.
I thought it was a novel idea. I thought it showed good faith on behalf of the communities, and I thought it would have showed good faith on the part of the government to say: "Those moneys are not going to go in some black hole, but because of the fact that they have been raised through noise violations, we will be pumping those moneys, or part of those moneys, back to the problem so that hopefully with the passage of time the situation will be ameliorated rather than aggravated".
A further point that we advanced in terms of an amendment was one that we also had recommended as part of a metropolitan Toronto Liberal caucus task force several years back, two years to be precise. The Liberal members of Parliament from metropolitan Toronto and area came up with what I thought was a very articulate and creative set of recommendations for the government in terms of combating and managing the problem of not only airport expansion but airport noise. One of the central recommendations that we put forward was the creation of an airport ombudsman, for lack of a better title.
The frustration we have right now is that when there is a noise violation and when a constituent or an individual homeowner wishes to complain, they usually pick up the telephone and one of two things happens. Either the line on the other end is busy or they get to talk to a tape recorder or an answering machine. That obviously causes a great deal of frustration because once again the complaint goes nowhere, the frustration and anxiety of a community increase, the confrontation therefore be-

Government Orders
tween that community and the airport or the airport manager is heightened and you have a situation that obviously spells some doom and gloom.
What we are talking about is the management of the problem, managing the reality of the noise complaints that invariably will come with the likes of an operation with the capacity of Pearson International Airport.
What we are talking about is being realistic. We did not wish to create titles for the sake of creating titles or spend money for the sake of spending money. What we wanted to do was improve the system. We wanted to improve the response. We wanted to let people know that somehow there was someone on the other end of the system cognizant of that frustration who could react to it. We wanted to systematically put something in place that would respond to it generically, rather than a tape recorder taking the distraught message at two o'clock in the morning that the windows were shattering because some airplane from Jamaica was coming in once again at Pearson International Airport.
If you are talking into a machine what is going to preclude another airliner, the next morning at two o'clock, from doing the same thing?
You have a situation in which there is a sense of helplessness out there. It is not only in this problem. It is basically rampant across the country in terms of that one citizen saying "What can we do in face of the system? Why should I vote? Does it make any difference?"
This ombudsman position would be symbolizing that the complaints are important because they will be monitored and become part of something or a pattern that we need to analyse and dissect in order to make life a little easier for those surrounding communities.
We talked about that in a task force report two years ago and I reintroduced the amendment at committee stage. It was ruled out of order in terms of being outside the purview of the bill, but once again I appeal to the minister and to the government benches not to lose sight of that role. It would not only help the people living around the airport but it would improve the administration and the headaches that the airport manager at Pearson International Airport has to deal with each and every day.
The other fact of life is the whole question of curfews. In a letter to me dated October 25 the Minister of State for Transport responded to my letter which I had raised on behalf of constituents in York West in terms of the noise problem. She said: "I must stress that there are no curfew hours at Pearson airport. However, large air carrier jet operations are restricted between midnight and seven in the morning".
There is a debate on whether curfews should be mandatory at an airport like Pearson. I fall on the side that they should. The line is that certain kinds of aircraft generation, the more modem ones, are more silent or quieter than the large DC-8 stretches. They are.
An average homeowner living around an airport has not seen an airplane yet that does not make a lot of noise. That is a fact of life. Because of the different generations of planes some are permitted to land between midnight and seven o'clock in the morning. Therefore it causes problems on a practical basis.
Individuals are awakened in the middle of the night on a regular basis by aircraft for one reason or another coming in at all the wee hours of the night. If we put ourselves in the shoes of those homeowners who need to get up at six in the morning to go and make an honest living, it would not be too much of a pleasure to get up at two, three, or four o'clock in the morning because of a number of aircraft coming in.
I ask the minister once again to take a hard look at the whole question of night curfews.
Canadians living around the airport understand situations such as an emergency landing, an extraordinary situation in which a plane is unable to take off from point a or needs to land in point b, or a situation involving the Red Cross. What they do not understand are situations which sometimes become more than the exception. To some of them aircraft travelling at all hours of the morning looks like the rule more than the exception.
I stress that we need to re-examine the whole question of curfews and whether they ought to be more strictly applied. I believe that the evidence points toward a much stricter enforcement of a curfew at the major international airports.
December 6, 1991

Another method of trying to manage the noise is the fair alternation, particularly at Pearson International Airport, of planes landing and taking off at the various runways. If I could take a moment to simply localize the problem, it is one that is particularly felt in the south end of my riding.
Whenever planes use runway 24L-06R as opposed to 24R-06L it means that the aircraft only fly over the Humberlea community, which is the whole south end of my riding. Those residents have not been asking for the elimination of 24L, the elimination of planes landing there when wind conditions are such that they have no other alternative, or the elimination of emergency landings on 24L. They are asking for a more or less equal alternation between 24L and 24R so that we are sharing the burden of the noise, rather than simply localizing it over one area.
There is no secret why a lot of aircraft use 24L. It happens to be the runway that is closest to the terminal. I know that aircraft wish to reduce their fuel consumption by taxiing for two minutes rather than 15 minutes. I understand that aircraft want to provide maximum convenience to their passengers by getting them into the terminal in under five minutes rather than taxiing for 15 minutes.
What the airport, the department and the airlines also have to understand is that if we are always going to land predominantly over one runway it means that one section of the entire affected area has the problem. That is unfair.
It is like taxes. Why is there a tax revolt? It is in part because taxes are a bit too high, they are up to here and we are living to pay government. However, there is also a feeling that some people are not pulling their weight and that some are pulling more than others. We are all prepared to pay our fair share, but when someone or some group does not that is when you get a revolt. Some of the shoulders of the working middle class are feeling inordinately heavier at this time.
It is the same in this situation. Why should the community of Humberlea in North York be saddled with most of the problem when we can to try share the problem of airport noise?
Government Orders
I have written the minister a number of times. I am pleased that she has responded, but the problem still exists. We need the minister and the department to strictly enforce the requirement with air traffic controllers and airline captains that there be an alternation between our runways and that planes not necessarily get to the terminal by the quickest and cheapest way. That is only one side of the equation. The other side happens to be the people who are burdened with the by-product of that noise problem.
I wish to thank the community groups that have come forward and testified. I would particularly like to thank Mr. John Doherty of the Council of Concerned Citizens, the Etobicoke Federation of Residents and Ratepayers Association, and acknowledge the concern that also has been expressed by groups in Mississauga and Humberlea, Mr. Gilbert Parrotta from the Humberlea Community Association, as well as Jack Sweet and Ted Wray from the Oakdale Residents Association. They have been vigilant in the face of a parliamentary secretary who dishonoured himself with a constant barrage of questions to these community groups, questioning their legitimacy or credibility, as did some officials of the department.
There was an article in The Mississauga News on October 16 in which the Director of Communications for Pearson International Airport, Mr. David Austin, basically inferred that it is: "Only a small clique of people who have problems with respect to noise", inferring that the majority around the airport are happy.
I can say that both the parliamentary secretary, with his cavalier attitude, and Mr. Austin, with this kind of allegation, are dead wrong. These community organizations have no vested interest other than that of representing the views, on a voluntary basis, of their neighbours and their communities. They have come forward in good faith to represent those individuals and get a fair shake. That is all they ask; no special treatment, just a fair shake.
On the Liberal side we not only accepted their testimony but asked them to testify. For a parliamentary secretary to question the credibility of community organizations at every turn does not do justice to a govern-

December 6, 1991
Government Orders
ment that says that it wishes to consult the public about all issues and decisions it has to take.
In summing up, I would like to say that Bill C-5, concerning the fines levied against airlines for noise violations, is good. However, that is only one aspect of a much wider battle we must wage in the war against airport noise for the benefit of Canadians who happen to have their castles in the communities that make up the hinterland of an airport.
We also need to take time when discussing airport expansion, management and transportation to be cognizant of those taxpayers. They are being fair and are being responsible. They are not asking for the demise of air travel. They are not asking for Pearson to close. They are simply asking us where we can, in whatever way we can, to balance the needs of a very complex society between the users of the airports and the residents who happen to live them.
I do not think that it is not an unfair request nor does it mean that it is impossible to come up with a solution. I think we are talking about the elements of a solution. It behoves Parliament and the government to look at them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on third reading of Bill C-5, an act to amend the Aeronautics Act and to amend an act to amend the Aeronautics Act.
I do so as a member of the Standing Committee on Transport which had the responsibility to review this legislation. At the outset I would like to echo the comments of the Minister of State for Transport and compliment my colleagues from all parties on that committee. I think we proved once again that Parliament and the parliamentary system can work.
The government brought forward a piece of legislation that was good to begin with. It had some flaws. We were able to correct one of those flaws by agreement of members of the committee. A clause that would have reduced the amount of notice for objections was returned to the original time period of 60 days to deal with the realities of northern Canada for the benefit of aviation operators up there who needed the extra time to find out what changes the government was making.
As has been pointed out, we also increased the level of fines for corporations that violate, among other things, noise pollution guidelines. We attempted to reduce the
fine to the individual because so often the individual is really just following company policy. If it is a pilot who is being told to ensure on-time delivery or being told by the company: "We do not care what the rules are, you have to land after a certain time or land more quickly" we did not feel that the level of punishment was appropriate. However, the government rejected that change. It did agree to increase the fine to $25,000.
The one change that really proves that this place can work is the one in which we, by unanimous consent, agreed to consider an amendment that was beyond the scope of the bill but was wanted by all parties, the government, and certainly by airline employees. That is a decision to give the government the right to regulate the hours of work of flight attendants. Currently the government has the right to regulate the hours of work of the front-end crew-the pilots, the engineers, the people who drive the plane-and it does that. It has prescribed a maximum work day of 15 hours.
Unfortunately flight attendants are not currently regulated. As we have found out, the flight attendants' prime responsibility is not the serving of food and drinks but ensuring our safety during take off and landing, both in terms of the in-cabin requirements of baggage stowage so that we have proper egress in the event of an emergency and making sure that we are wearing our seat belts, but also during an emergency landing and evacuation when it is their job to get us out of that plane safely.
I want to put on the record two examples that show why regulation is needed and why we cannot leave it to the collective agreement process to decide on these matters.
The first is the case of Nationair 10. On December 3, 1990 Nationair flight 680 left Mirabel at 0900 hours. It arrived at Fort Lauderdale at 1230. This aircraft and its crew were scheduled to begin the return flight to Mirabel at 1430 and finally arrived at Mirabel at approximately 1730 on the same day. This would have meant a total duty day of about 9.5 hours.
The return flight was boarded in Fort Lauderdale at 1400 hours. The captain then announced a 45-minute delay because extra meals had to be brought aboard as there were more passengers than expected. It was not long before passengers noticed mechanics working on one of the engines. This began a series of events that led to the flight attendants determining that they were too fatigued to handle safety situations properly. This was

partially due to the extreme agitation and stress symptoms being exhibited by the passengers as well as by their own physical state and exhaustion. It was aggravated by the pilot's own lack of understanding of the situation and his state of mind, probably brought on by his extremely long duty day.
The crew had spent the entire day on duty dealing with concerned and agitated passengers. The passengers were boarded and deplaned three times in total and they were kept for most of the time on board an aircraft that had no air conditioning. They were also not informed of the real reasons for the delay.
As a result, the passengers were extremely agitated on a number of occasions. Some became so overwrought that they were literally screaming to be let off. Some, in their eagerness to get off, left without their luggage. Others waited on the jet way, smoking. By the time the captain ordered the crew to shut the doors and leave behind any passengers not aboard the aircraft this particular pilot had already been on duty for at least 16.5 hours. He had a further three to four hours ahead of him. He was in a very stressed condition. Some flight attendants were so concerned about his ability to make decisions that this became a major reason for their refusal to operate the flight.
It subsequently was revealed that the flight was not mechanically fit to leave in any event. The mechanical problem was serious enough that specialized help was needed and the engine could not be fixed until the next day. The departure would have also violated security regulations specifying that luggage had to match the passengers on board. A number of passengers had already left the airport and the pilot wanted to leave others standing on the jet way while their luggage was still on board.
After exercising their right to refuse when they were ordered by their pilot to work a total of 18.5 hours, and possibly more, in a single continuous duty period, the 10 flight attendants were fired. Nationair is now suing each of them for the amount of money it claimed to have lost because of their refusal to work, over $120,000 each.
That is one example of the realities of the industry that demonstrates why it cannot be left to the collective agreement process to provide protection, not just for the
Government Orders
workers but for all who travel, whether it is on Nationair, Air Canada, Canadian or what have you.
The second example I want to read into the record is dated January 1990. It is a letter addressed to the Canadian Union of Public Employees and the Ministry of Transport, as well as to another individual.
To Whom It May Concern:
I am writing to you with safety concerns of a flight I operated earlier this month.
On January 8, I was scheduled to work Vancouver to Honolulu, check in was 8.15 a.m. At approximately 2030 on January 7,1 received a call from Crew Scheduling informing me that I would now be deadheading to Winnipeg, working Winnipeg to Vancouver, then Vancouver to Honolulu, and that the flight was departing at 3.15 a.m. January 8. Briefing at 2.15, less than six hours notice. By the time I packed and made two phone calls it was 2130.1 fell asleep sometime after 2230, and had to wake at 1 a.m. The Winnipeg flight was two hours and twenty minutes of which I dozed for, at the most one and a half hours.
When landing in Vancouver, and finding out that the company had no intention of replacing us, my thought was that I would not make it. We took off from Vancouver at 11 a.m. I almost fell asleep in my jumpseat. Three hours into the flight, I felt like I was in a dream, everything was in slow motion. If there had been a fire, or a medical emergency, I really don't know how fast I could have reacted. By the time we landed in Honolulu, I had at the most 4 hours sleep in 32 hours. I thought to myself: "Please get us down safely". It was all I could do to stay awake.
It is frightening to experience feeling totally useless when you know that a lot of lives could depend on you. What is even more frightening is knowing that the front end crew were also in the same situation. After the flight I asked them how much sleep they had, the flight engineer said 2 hours.
I feel we were lucky this time, but when will our luck run out? At what cost are we placing our passengers' lives? I'm sure you will recognize this situation as a potential safety hazard and do everything you can to prevent it from happening again.
The transport committee and this House has acted. I say thanks on behalf of all of those men and women who look after our safety in the skies and on the ground for the work that they do in protecting us. I say thanks to the House of Commons, the minister, her staff, the department and the Official Opposition for accepting my motion to give the government the power to regulate hours of work of flight attendants. It is in our own best interests.
I have one final comment. The next step in this after the other place considers this bill is the drafting of regulations. I know that will be a matter of negotiations

December 6, 1991
Government Orders
between the Air Transport Association, Canadian Union of Public Employees and the Government of Canada.
I would urge the other place to give speedy passage to Bill C-5.1 would urge the minister and her staff to give speedy consideration to the negotiation of the hours of work of the flight attendants because it is in all of our interests that that law be put in place as quickly as possible and the regulations that implement it be drafted and gazetted. We know that will take some time but the sooner we get at it the better it will be because we do not want this question at the bargaining table. I have already been told that Air Canada is planning on trying to negotiate a longer length of day at the next round in September.
The clock is ticking. I urge the government to act very quickly.
Once again I say thanks. It has really been a good day for Parliament and an even better day for airline employees.

Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the House leaders that I will be very brief. I will try and make this less than two minutes because I respect the fact that we are trying to get this bill through the House of Commons by 1 p.m.
I do want to support everything that the Minister of Transport has said today as well as my colleague for York South-Weston and the member from the New Democratic Party. But I must put on the record that the problems with noise abatement are not just with our major airports in this country.

Pearson while the problems in terms of noise and hours of work at some of the smaller airports are being forgotten. As you know, that artery goes right through the centre of a heavily populated urban area. So I am going to be happy to report to my citizens' group this weekend that thanks to the efficiency of this House the

subtopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It is with great pleasure once again that I return to the four bills which are before us. The bills of course are C-4, C-19, C-28 and C-34. They are bills which relate to the regulations and rules which will redefine the powers and ownership structures of Canadian financial institutions.
We are looking at some major legislation here which had a beginning back in 1985 through the report of the McDougall green paper, in 1986 with the Hockin blue paper, the draft trust bill which was in December of 1987 and furthermore the Canadian Senate report of 1992 which was titled Towards a National Market and Finance Services.
Previously I had said that this is a bill where we put our best minds together, supposedly where we worked on the studying of 2,428 clauses relating to these four bills and where we had a great deal of potential to actually create a major improvement in the way we regulate financial institutions.

subtopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: We did.

subtopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I hear already from the other side from the hon. member for Mississauga East, I believe, that we did. I disagree. I think we did not. I think we had a great chance to show average Canadians that we were on their side. Unfortunately we came up with mediocre legislation. As a matter of fact I was referring to how my colleague, the member for Nickel Belt, had referred to the member for Mississauga. The member for Mississauga had been the chairman of the committee. He was dressed-I am speaking rhetorically-in his wizard's costume with his wizard's hat. He churned the cauldron in order to make this brew for financial regulations. He said that we could not put anything more into it and that these changes would not be allowed. "We do not want to have pro-Canadian consumer type legislation".
I am sure my hon. colleague will say: "Now wait a minute, Phil, it is a question of who you consider to be consumers. Trust companies and banks and such institutions are consumers and we have to look out for their interests as well." To a certain extent I would say that is true but I believe that the interests we are looking out
Government Orders
for mainly are not the consumers' interests but in a very large sense-larger than necessary-they are the interests of the large corporations.
It seems that the elephant has given birth to a mouse and the mouse is a very mediocre one at that. I do want to say some positive things though about the bill because there are some things that are good in it.
We welcome Bill C-34 which is an act to revise and amend the law governing co-operative credit associations. Coming from Quebec it would be unthinkable to be against a bill which would improve the situation of our caisses populaires for example.

I was quite surprised and pleased that a few of my colleagues pointed out that the caisses populaires are not limited to Quebec. The caisses populaires movement and Mr. Rouleau's group also exist in all the other provinces.

subtopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: There are also the Caisses Populaires Desjardins.

subtopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Yes, I know. But for the caisses populaires in general, I understand that 1,400 branches hold assets of nearly $44 billion. Moreover, the caisses populaires are the largest employer in Quebec.
It is for that reason I congratulate the government on its efforts to regulate the caisses populaires so as to better harmonize their activities, and make them more deeply rooted in the community.
We support the clauses of the bill that deal with consumer protection and the way that the review committee or the protection committee, which is called the audit committee, was set up. It is good that some regulations stipulate that the majority of the members of these committees must not be affiliated with the company's directors.
We are especially pleased to see that the members of this review committee or shareholders interest protection committee are independent individuals, because that is extremely important. Madam Speaker, I do not know if you ever attended a board of directors meeting as a shareholder and were not overly pleased with the information that you got from so-called independent individuals, from people who could have informed you

Government Orders
on the financial condition of your organization-maybe it is a caisse populaire, I do not know-because the people who provided you with the information and the organization itself were not independent or open enough.
I believe that we have really taken a step forward with this bill in that the people who will inform us of the true condition of these financial institutions must have a certain independence.
There are some good things in these four bills that deal with financial institutions, but there are also certain flaws. My political party and I, as a member of Parliament, are not at all pleased that this reform plan contained in the four bills fails to deal with the harmonization of our domestic markets and our regulatory authorities, which are fragmented.
I think that because of deregulation, we are seeing a kind of wheeling and dealing between jurisdictions. Madam Speaker, I know you are aware of the differences between the way federal and provincial jurisdictions approach financial institutions. Sometimes the companies end up totally confused. Federal regulations are so strict that these companies do not know what to do, and sometimes they practically have to seek the protection of various provincial jurisdictions. For instance, in Quebec the regulations for insurance companies are not the same as the federal regulations.
This is not to say that one is better than the other, but there are differences. There is no harmonization, and it is because of this lack of harmonization that insurance companies or other companies may face a lot of problems. I find that intolerable, especially considering the increased emphasis on sensible consultation. It is quite simple, really. We just put our heads together and say: Well, how can we accommodate the companies? Can we accommodate the wishes and the needs of the general public and at the same time protect the public?
I think we can, but in this bill-actually we are talking about four different bills-we have failed to harmonize what should have been harmonized. I think we could have done better. For instance, in addition to the bills that have already been introduced, this government could have introduced a bill that would allow banks to sell insurance. This is no big deal! In Quebec, they have been doing it for ages at the Caisses Populaires Desjardins. They sell insurance.
As a former president of the Automobile Protection Association, I supported the Mouvement Desjardins in this respect because I thought it would make the industry more competitive in Quebec and, as a result, reduce the cost of insurance-yes, competitive-and also make all parties in the insurance industry more responsive to their customers.
That is exactly what happened. It didn't happen overnight, but for almost ten years, the Caisses Populaires Desjardins have been competing in the insurance industry because in Quebec, they are allowed to sell insurance contracts, including automobile insurance, to their customers. A number of my constituents in Chamb-ly wrote to tell me they felt prices were very competitive at the Caisses Populaires Desjardins, and they were also very satisfied with the service they received. Even when they compared the Caisses Populaires with insurance companies elsewhere, they felt it was very healthy to have the caisses populaires compete in the insurance sales field.
Interestingly the predecessor of these four bills was Bill C-93, which ended up being split into the bills now before the House: C-4, C-19, C-28 and C-34.
I may have given the wrong number for the bill, and the hon. member for Mississauga may be able to help me shortly. Originally there was a clause to allow banks to sell insurance, and I hope that my colleague will agree with me, because I read it. They had the right to sell insurance. But today, I do not know, maybe because of our sorcerer's apprentice with his sort of soup made in a cauldron, we do not have this clause to allow banks to sell insurance. I am disappointed, because people often say that is plain common sense. Even we in the NDP would like to see competition and we found it was an excellent suggestion from the federal government, from this government, to have a clause in this bill allowing banks to sell insurance, because the Caisses Populaires Desjardins have not abused their right to sell it. Service has improved as a result of this competition. But unfortunately somewhere, for some reason, I do not know, this government which advocates and wants to promote competition and to protect consumers has refused to allow banks to sell insurance to their customers.

One of my Liberal colleagues says "fortunately". I think that it is unfortunate. If it works well in Quebec, it can also work well in other places. It is plain common sense, no more and no less.
We could have done better, as one of my colleagues already pointed out. We could have required credit card issuers to calculate interest differently, in the way that the hon. member for Mississauga suggested to us in his Bill C-236, I believe. This bill would have credit card issuers calculate interest only on the unpaid balance rather than on the whole amount borrowed. This means that if you owed $500 on a credit card and paid $250, the issuer could charge interest only on the unpaid $250.

speechtext: They wanted to do that!

speechtext:
No, they did not want to do that. It is too pro-consumer, too revolutionary, if I may say so. It may have been too NDP for this government, I do not know. I would say that their approach does not make much sense, since most of our constituents are in favour of our proposal. I am sure that most hon. members agree that when the government proposed these four bills to protect us, to help us, to regulate financial institutions, it forgot to protect the people at the bottom. Is it an oversight? I prefer to say that it is. I am not talking about the banks and other financial institutions; I am talking about people like us who use credit cards.
Even if we pay $250 on a total of $500, we still have to pay interest on that $500 today. That is disgusting, unacceptable, anti-consumer, illogical and unfortunately, it is really sad to see a government omit or overlook such a thing.

I am disappointed by these four proposed bills. I compared rhetorically my hon. colleague, to the grand wizard putting into his cauldron, his soup, all these different resolutions, all these 2,400 and some clauses, supposedly harmonizing the system, which it does not. I believe it creates a more favourable atmosphere for the large corporations to merge. Rather than making the system work better, I think it is going to work less so.
The government could have done better. It could have done much more to protect both institutions as well as
Government Orders
everyday Canadians. I am sad because I think the bill had great potential. We could have done so many things and we did not.
The government is always asking: "NDP, Edmonston, Audrey McLaughlin, give us some examples. What would you do?"
Initially I said I would lower interest rates. I would lower interest rates on credit cards. Take a look at the credit cards. The minister said he had. He did no such thing. Take a look at the prime. The prime has hit an 18 year low. It is low. What are credit cards at?
When the minister of consumer affairs is asked what he is going to do about the difference in credit card interest rates and the prime rate, which is over 10 percentage points, the minister says-now follow me because this is logic which I am not quite sure I understand; it is very short, I am just giving a resume here-"The costs associated with their use are varied and complex and consumers should consider other more favourable forms of credit".

subtopic: CO-OPERATIVE CREDIT ASSOCIATIONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Like what?

Is that not throwing in the towel? Is that not saying: "I am sorry, I am the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs but really I am the minister of corporate affairs". That is what he is saying. "I cannot help you. Go someplace else".
Finally what I am saying, Madam Speaker, is that the government could have done much more. It could have been much more evolutionary. I am not even asking it to be revolutionary. When we look at Bill C-4, Bill C-19, Bill C-28, and Bill C-34, unfortunately the government elephant laboured long and hard but it gave birth to a mouse and a mediocre one at that.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague from the riding of Malpeque on her hard work, along with other members of the committee from all sides of the House, as well as her work with the government side in order to make sure that this bill will become a reality.
For the record I would like to give her credit for her work, especially in the area of consumer protection, to ensure that there is a complaint mechanism put in as part of this bill. I would like to congratulate the government on adopting this proposal in their bill.

Government Orders
As a result, we have a fairly good bill that, hopefully, the House will approve and send to the Senate as quickly as possible.
Having said that, Madam Speaker, I discussed with the hon. member her views on this proposal and asked her about some of the amendments she tried to introduce. She brought to my attention a fairly impressive amendment. I would like to say that I was somewhat surprised that the government would decide not to proceed with her proposal.
The amendment deals with the use of plain language when it comes to trust companies or banking industries putting out information to the consumers or to their customers. I understand that the government is resisting because it feels it might be a little late to adopt such a proposal.
I would like to suggest that perhaps while the bill is on its way to the Senate the government side could consult with the Senate and make sure that it adopts such a good, interesting and very well balanced proposal.
I would suggest that my colleague from Malpeque, Prince Edward Island does her research very well. Obviously she has looked at other places here in Canada as well as in North America before she made her proposal. She informed me that Alberta already has legislation on the books although there is still a bit of work to be done before it will become an effective law. Also she has informed me that in New York there has been legislation which allows the use of plain language and it seems to be working extremely well.
I am quite surprised that the government decided not to adopt such a proposal in light of the fact that more and more the Canadian public is aware of the need for plain language, whether we are talking about politicians communicating with their constituents or whether we are talking about regulations being put into place.
The reason why that use of plain language is extremely important is because, as you know, Madam Speaker, with an illiteracy rate of approximately 38 to 40 per cent, one could not help but say: "The least we can do, when we are trying to communicate with the people and make their life a little simpler, is provide them with information that is useful and that can be read easily".
Having said that, I would like to move on now to speak about banking and its relationship with consumers and the financial situation that we are faced with here in Canada. I cannot help but address the question of the over-all picture rather than focusing on the narrow end of what we have before us in terms of legislation.
The legislation is good. The proposal is excellent. We would like to see amendments made to it but if that is not feasible perhaps over the next few years we will be able to deal with those amendments in a little more effective way. However, we have to look at what we have before us in terms of the industry and its relation to consumers.
First I would like to say that we should be all very happy and optimistic about the fact that our banking industry is one of the best banking industries in North America, perhaps anywhere around the world. All of the credit should go both to regulators as well as to the industry itself. The industry has played a leadership role in weeding out any kind of potential difficulties. The regulators have been working in conjunction with the industry over the years trying to co-operatively come up with proposals that are not only satisfactory to the banking industry but also protect the interests of consumers.
What we have seen with the government proposal is another good example of the co-operative work that has taken place between both the private sector and the government sector in this field.
Looking at the banking situation or the financial situation I cannot help but look at the people who are using our banking industry over the past few months and indicate that there is a reason for us to stop and take note of the kind of difficulties that exist out in the community.
Going back just a little to November 20,1 would like to bring to your attention a statement made by Canada's chief financial services regulator who appeared to be a little pessimistic about the weak economy. In his speech Mr. Mackenzie, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, told his audience that due to the situation in housing, real estate and retailing, "there is a deep pessimism going through the banking community that I work with".

I thought at the time it was a rather strange coincidence that if we have to paint a realistic picture of what is going on, if we have to build public confidence, if we have to move aggressively in controlling inflation and reducing interest rates and injecting more life into the economy, that a statement like this would be made.
I put my hand on a piece of information that was published by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It deals with bankruptcies for the month of October 1991. During that month, you will be unhappy to learn, we had a total of 974 bankruptcies. That includes areas such as the manufacturing industry, construction, transportation, storage, communications and other utility industries, the wholesale trade industry, industries that deal with retail sales as well as business service industries, among others. In fact, there is in excess of about 20 different groups.
The annual bankruptcies to date are about 8,000, of which approximately 1,800 have taken place in the retail industries. There is in excess of 1,200 in the construction industry, about 700 in the manufacturing industry, 474 in the business service industry and so on.
I took those figures and I thought well, these seem to be the major areas where we have large numbers of companies going bankrupt. In particular, the bankruptcies are in the construction and manufacturing industries. I compared it to the statement which was made by Michael Mackenzie, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, that there seemed to be a deep pessimism going through the banking community. I think he was referring to the fact that there are a large number of bankruptcies taking place in those industries that really deal with banking. As you know, Madam Speaker, when an industry manufactures wood or steel or whatever component that is to be used in the construction industry, the construction industry will build homes and the consumer will go out and buy those homes. As a result of that, he or she might go to a bank in order to borrow money.
So the wheel of the Canadian economy in a lot of ways is as good as the wheel of the construction industry as well as industry as a whole. So whenever there is a deficiency in the construction industry, you will know that is a bad indication and is a cause for alarm.

As I mentioned, I looked at those figures and I went to a fairly recent report published by the Economic Council of Canada to look at the exports and export-dependent employment dynamic services here in Canada. I looked at the export share of total output in terms of the percentage.
To give an indication, when we look at areas such as rail, truck and other transportation and storage industries and combine the total in those areas in terms of employment, in excess of 60 per cent of all jobs are export related jobs.
If we look at bankruptcies in Canada, in the transportation industry as well as related industries, we find that out of about 8,000 industries about 600 have gone bankrupt.
Moving on to wholesale and trade, there is about 11.8 per cent export share of total output in terms of jobs in the export trade. The total number of industries in the retail sector that went under is about 1,800, that is out of about 8,000 bankruptcies so far in the industry.
By looking at those two components by themselves, one can see immediately that many of those companies which trade internationally are creating jobs locally. When those corporations are having difficulties and are going under, automatically the jobs that are provided by those companies are going to disappear.
All I wanted to do was give an idea of the fact that while there are a large number of jobs here in Canada that depend to a large extent on the amount of trade our industries are doing abroad, the better we equip those industries to do well abroad, the more protection we will have for the jobs here in Canada.
The bankruptcy figures show that a large number of corporations are going under and the other book which was published by the Economic Council of Canada, 1990, indicated the vast majority of those jobs actually deal with exports. We will automatically come to the conclusion that in order for us to deal with the socio-economic problem we presently have here in Canada, we have to improve the situation for those very same companies that are trading abroad.

That brings me to the nasty subject of the high dollar value. I would suggest that we could spin our wheels for as long as we want, but unless we come up with a proper policy that deals with or balances the value of the Canadian dollar as well as the inflation in Canada, we are not going to be able in the short term to turn the wheel of the economy in such a way that we can move forward and address the question of high unemployment and the question of slow economic growth.
To that extent there is a direct correlation between economic renewal here in Canada and the reduction of the value of the dollar so we can allow those companies to compete internationally and protect those jobs.
In the city of Ottawa, for example, if we look at the figures from January to October 1990, we had approximately 1,230 bankruptcies.

My colleague from Toronto says it is a shame. It is a shame. The picture gets even more bleak when it is compared to 1991. Here in our region we had in excess of 1,748 bankruptcies. That is an excess of 500 more bankruptcies than we had last year.
In the province of Ontario in the past 12 months, from November 1990 to October 1991, there were a total of 25,414 bankruptcies.
The picture in Ontario is no different from the picture all across Canada. For example, for the same period you will be disappointed to learn that over the past 12 months, from November of 1990 to October 1991, we had in Canada in excess of 64,052 bankruptcies. That is not a good picture.
I do not like to bring bad news always to the attention of the Canadian public or to the attention of my colleagues in the House of Commons, but I want to take this opportunity to say that while the federal government has a responsibility to address the value of the Canadian dollar and balance it with a controlled inflation rate, I want to turn a little bit to the province of Ontario. The government has done a disastrous job when it comes to dealing with a proper strategy for proper economic growth in the province of Ontario.
Last month, for example, Ontario business bankruptcies soared to a dismal 315 after a slight decline in September, and personal bankruptcies jumped to 2,782 from a 2,369 figure a month before. The total bankruptcies have increased by up to 17.4 per cent.
If you ask me why that is, I would say that there is only one simple reason: the NDP government of Ontario has deceived the people of Ontario on two fronts. Going into the election, it promised the world to the people of Ontario, with the hope that the people of Ontario believed it and saw in it an alternative at the time. Were they ever deceived. The government had a majority and as a result of that the business community had a lot of issues, a lot of bones to pick with the government.
The government as soon as it was elected had a look at the situation and said "We cannot deliver". That is fine if it came to the public and told the public that it cannot deliver on promises it made. As a result, the business community could move on with the realization that the NDP government of Ontario, which misled the electorate in the past election, cannot deliver on its promises. The business community could start investing in Ontario.
As it is now, it is a catch-22 for the business community. On the one hand, it is not too sure about what to expect from the province of Ontario and so it is not investing. On the other hand, on a daily basis we are seeing bankruptcy after bankruptcy taking place all across this province.
It is time for the government of Ontario to stand up and tell the people of Ontario that it is not going to be able to deliver on the promises made in the past election: "We fooled you".
The end result is that we could perhaps, as one of the largest provinces in this country and as one of the provinces that used to be one of the richest in this country, get on with our lives, both as the public and as the business community, and start investing in the economy.
I am saying all of this to demonstrate that by no means can we just blame the federal government for the lack of initiative when it comes to the high dollar policy.
I think a big part of the blame has to go to the largest province in Canada and that is the province of Ontario. I
