speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can understand why the hon. member from Windsor felt it was necessary to come to the defence of his leader in the province of Ontario. He did not do a very good job but he did the best that he could with the subject.
The bill before us is probably one of the most complicated bills with which this Parliament has ever had to deal. It is a long awaited overhaul of Canada's major financial institutions.
I know of no subject which is more complex in terms of the details involved. This is because of the evolving nature of our financial industries.
In the good old days, perhaps a decade ago, there were the so-called four pillars: banks, trust and loan companies, insurance companies and security dealers. Everybody knew what those institutions did more or less. They worked in discrete, isolated areas and they were not competitors. Each sector had a partial or sometimes a complete monopoly in its own field.
Over the last decade or so, the barriers between our four major types of financial institutions have been broken down. They have merged into each other's businesses. The law we see today is a recognition of the breakdown of those four pillars. The point is not whether we want to go back a decade to the way things were when it was more simple because we cannot go back, the barriers have been broken.
The bill we see before us does not eradicate all of the walls. Some of the four pillars are still maintained. Not
all of the financial institutions can go into the business of all of the other financial institutions. That is why there is so much complexity in this law and why it is so difficult for us, as members of Parliament, to say: "My goodness, we have done the perfect job".
We have to be humble in what we have been able to achieve because when these barriers are breaking down there are always going to be some institutions claiming that we were not fair to them, that they were not able to get into certain areas that others can, that they do not have the competitive advantages that other institutions have.
Having approached this bill with a certain degree of humility, because of the difficulty of bringing the law up to date with the economic realities of the 1990s, let us also congratulate the members of the committee who worked so hard to make these bills possible. I want to go on record to congratulate our member for Malpeque who has taken a very hard working and constructive role in this entire debate.
There are three main aims of this new legislation. One is to provide better services to the borrowers and depositors in these institutions, to owners. Second is to ensure the safety and soundness of these financial institutions. The third objective is to ensure that in the global view our institutions can be competitive both domestically and internationally.
Let us look at the first of these objectives, better service. In the time available I cannot go into all aspects of this objective, but I want to touch on a couple of them. Does this bill deal with the interest rates that can be charged to users of credit cards? Today in Canada the prime rate is 8 per cent, the lowest it has been in 18 years. Thank goodness it has come down. Thank goodness the government has brought it down, because it was this government that put the rate up so high in the first place.
Have the interest rates on credit cards come down? They are now in the range of 19 per cent and higher. This is an enormous spread and I have not heard enough evidence in this House to justify why these high rates must be paid by credit card users.
This bill does not deal with it and that is an obvious deficiency in this bill.

Another area in terms of better service to the public is addressed by a bill that was introduced by the member for Malpeque. She was able, with the co-operation of government and opposition members, to have it passed. If customers have a complaint they now have a statutory right to go to their financial institution and make that complaint, and if the financial institution does not respond they can then go to the superintendent. This is now written into the law. It is an empowerment of consumers to help ensure that they are treated fairly by these regulated institutions.
As for safety and soundness, I again want to commend the member for Malpeque who brought in Motion No. 47. This again was agreed to by all members of this House. It is an amendment to the bill at a very late stage which encourages employees to come forward and report on accounting procedures. It says they will not be penalized in any way if they go to the auditors and explain things which possibly management or the institution itself do not want the auditors to know.
This is important in ensuring the soundness of our financial institutions because we had testimony before us that, had the proper accounting procedures been used, we might not have had the Standard Trust disaster. We might have been able to avoid the problems that occurred in our two western banks.
The more that individuals can be encouraged to come forward and be forthright with the auditors, to put the auditors on notice, the more it will contribute to the soundness of our financial institutions, which exist not only to serve their owners but the public as a whole.
We cannot claim total success in terms of updating this legislation because there is still a certain anomaly which exists, and maybe this was inevitable. There are trust and loan companies in this country which are bigger than banks which in effect take deposits and make loans.
However, unlike banks they do not have to be widely held. Parliament in its wisdom said that banks must be widely held in order to avoid some of the conflicts of interest that may arise from time to time.
This was one of the very difficult issues for us to deal with because there are some very large trust and loan companies and they are being very well and soundly
Government Orders
managed. However, they have sprung up under single ownership.
I am sure that the question we are going to have to come back to within a couple of years is whether, because banks must be widely held, with no one owning more than 10 per cent of the shares, the same requirement should be imposed on trust and loan companies. The bill did not deal with this particular aspect.
Another area which is probably beyond us as the Parliament of Canada, but which is highly regrettable, is the whole issue of regulation of our financial institutions. There are federal loan and trust companies, federal banks, and provincial loan and trust companies. There can be a federal loan and trust company doing business in the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario seeks to regulate under its own laws those trust and loan companies, and the Ontario laws may be totally or somewhat different from the federal laws in certain areas.
In addition to that, Ontario will regulate the federal loan or trust company's business, not only in the province of Ontario but right across Canada.
If we are going to have safety we also need efficiency of regulation. That means harmonization of our federal and provincial laws as they relate to our financial institutions. We are a country of 26 million people. If we want to be competitive does it make sense that we should have .11 different laws regulating these financial institutions? Surely, in the interest of efficiency and competitiveness, as Canadians we could find a way to regulate our major financial institutions at only one level. This is a goal that we as a Parliament and we as Canadians from coast to coast should be seeking to achieve.
The third goal of which I spoke is that of international competitiveness. Here we get into the issue of what foreign financial institutions should be able to do in Canada. What can they do? I have never been completely convinced that by opening up Canada to total competition from abroad for our financial institutions that we were helping strengthen our own financial institutions or that we were better equipping our financial institutions to compete here in Canada or in foreign jurisdictions.
When we changed the Bank Act in the early 1980s to increase the number of Schedule B, Schedule II or foreign banks coming into Canada from a very small

December 6, 1991
Government Orders
number to something like 60 I remember wondering at that time what we were doing. Were we allowing these foreign banks to come into Canada to cream off some of the top accounts, the multinationals, the ones with connections outside this country that had lots of security outside Canada, and leaving the homeowners, the farmers, and the small businesses for the Canadian banks? I was quite worried about that.
When Parliament in its wisdom passed the law to allow the foreign banks to come in here we on the finance committee said at that time: "Let us be sure we monitor these foreign banks to make sure they are not just cherry picking, to make sure they are increasing the competitiveness and to make sure they are doing their fair share in terms of small business, farmers and homeowners".
I regret to say that type of monitoring has not been carried out. Therefore, I think one of the expectations, which was greater competitiveness with the benefits filtering down to the smaller borrowers, was denied to us.
Did this opening up of Canada to more competition from foreign banks give us greater access to other countries in the world? The main country we are concerned with is the United States. Did we, by opening up Canada to American banks get a greater right for Canadian banks to compete in the United States? As a result of the free trade deal which took down additional barriers, did we get the same type of rights in the United States that we gave Americans in Canada? No, the member for Burlington is absolutely wrong. We did not get reciprocal treatment for our banks in the United States to American banks in Canada. What we received was national treatment. National treatment is very different from reciprocity. Let me explain this.
By allowing American banks to come into Canada, they get access to nation-wide branch banking. They can set up their branch banks right across this country. Did Canada get that right in the United States? No.
Just recently a bill passed Congress that we had hoped would grant Canadian banks branch banking across the United States. We did not get it. So as for reciprocity American banks in Canada can have branch banks
nation-wide while Canadian banks in the United States cannot. That is lack of reciprocity number one.
Lack of reciprocity number two is that U.S. banks own securities dealers, a company like American Express. We can say it is not a bank but they own large securities dealers. Can Canadian banks go down to the United States and own a securities dealer? No. We have real problems with that.
The third area is that under this new legislation that we brought in we have American banks in Canada that own insurance and trust companies. Can Canadian banks going to the United States own savings and loan or insurance companies or trust companies down there? In other words with this bill the reciprocity gap that existed previous to this bill for Canadian financial institutions vis-a-vis American banks has been widened. How does this lead to enhanced competitiveness?
I am also disappointed that this bill did not deal with what I think is probably the greatest travesty in terms of the administration of our financial institutions and which I think is a blight on our reputation for being an even-handed and fair rule of law nation. With the granting to American Express of the AMEX Bank of Canada licence and breaching five out of the nine guidelines set by this government, Canada showed the world community that friends are granted rights and privileges not available to anyone else.
We have spoken a number of times about what went on and how the pressure came from American Express. Through its massive support of the government in the last election on free trade, American Express lobbied to open up the border for financial services. American Express did not want to qualify as a bank in the United States for U.S. purposes because had it qualified as a bank it would have had to get rid of its major securities company. It was not regulated as a bank in the United States.
It was probably because of the tremendous support given to the government by American Express that this government was prepared to breach five of its own nine guidelines to allow that bank licence to be issued. This is even after our diligent public servants in Canada had held the application up for about 27 months.

Does this bill do anything to deal with this type of issue? No. If American Express were to apply today they would still be in breach of five of the nine guidelines.
All I can say is thank goodness that this bill does not retroactively legitimize what was a terrible breach of trust toward the Canadian people by this government. It was a granting of benefits to friends. It was a benefit which it would not have given to anyone else. Thank goodness this bill does not legitimize retroactively that type of operation. Neither does it go far enough to deal with a government that may choose again in the future to be arbitrary and to favour its friends at the expense of all other people who apply in honesty and good faith and in the expectation that Canada is a country in which the rule of law applies and it will be applied equally and fairly to all applicants.
This bill cannot be considered to be the be all and the end all. There are many issues which have not been resolved. It has been a good human attempt to deal with what I think is one of the most intellectually complex areas in the world. This is because of the breakdown of the old four pillars and the melding of them and our attempt to achieve equity and balance among those four within Canada. We have attempted to deal with the new realities, at the same time ensuring that the needs of customers, borrowers and depositors will be met. At the same time, we have attempted to ensure the soundness and the safety of these institutions because more than anything else Canada's banking reputation must rest on a sound basis and sense of security. That is why we cannot have any more of the AMEX bank licences because that makes us look like a banana republic.
This bill does attempt to deal with the competitiveness issue both within Canada, among these four institutions competing against foreigners and outside Canada with the ability of these institutions to compete abroad.
My feeling is that where we have not made the best of this bill is in this competitiveness area. There are people in Canada who still feel-and I am one of them-that foreign financial institutions have greater privileges in Canada than we are getting in their countries. I will end immediately. We have seen only a decade ago that our banks were among the top in terms of assets on a global basis. We now are lucky to have one in the top fifty. We have a long way to go. Let us as a country take steps to

ensure that our banks and financial institutions serve the purposes of which we have spoken.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to resist the temptation to respond to the previous member about the sins and inequities of his brother in power. It probably is not worth pursuing that subject further.
What I would like to do seriously is to congratulate the committee which worked on this legislation. I want to particularly congratulate the member for Nickel Belt who has been our representative through what has been an extremely difficult marathon slog of four pieces of complex legislation. Each piece had many different interested parties which wanted to have their say. It has been a difficult process for all members of that committee. I congratulate them.
Since he is in the House I want to say that the chairman who is the member for Mississauga South did an excellent job in this particular case. He was previously on the finance committee and now he is chair of the subcommittee or legislative committee, I forget which, that took on this bill in this session. He was better known as the terminator from GST days. We have however a set of bills in front of us which put into effect three important philosophies. We have first and perhaps most important a new philosophy which says that we will permit financial institutions in this country to be much more interconnected than has been the case previously. It will be possible for banks to own insurance companies and for insurance companies to own trust companies. There is an attempt to erect supposed walls in the actual operation of these institutions but, frankly, I am sceptical about whether those walls will be as soundproof and as hermetically sealed as the people who brought this legislation forward suggest. I think not. I think we are going to see much more in the way of conglomeration of our financial institutions.
The second piece of philosophy which marks these three bills is much more emphasis on self-policing in the regulation of these institutions. That too is something which the government has defended strongly but something which in my view carries with it considerable risks. There is a risk that the self-policing will not be done. We have seen in this country recently a series of unfortunate events with respect to both banks and trust companies. We have seen the collapse of two of our western banks.

Government Orders
We have seen the takeover and shut-down of the Bank of Credit and Commerce which was a foreign-owned bank which was implicated in a whole series of scandals and fraudulent activities in other parts of the world. We have seen the collapse of Standard Trust. We have seen the teetering on the brink which is taking place with Central Guaranty Trust which just announced this week that it is selling 25 of its branches because of financial pressures.
In the cases that we have been able to probe into in places like the finance committee we have discovered that there have been serious problems. We found in the case of the Bank of Credit and Commerce here in Canada for instance that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation's rules were not followed in all cases in that foreign bank's operations here in Canada. We found in the case of a number of the trust companies which have been affected by financial pressures in recent years that loans had in fact been made which put into effect investments that could not be justified by the extent of the loan or the riskiness of the venture which was being supported.
In some cases we have been dealing with the collapse of the real estate market. That has been the case especially in Alberta and a major piece of the explanation of the bankruptcy of those two banks in that part of our country.'
That has not been the only problem. There has been a failure to recognize the need for strict financial security. Despite this experience and despite the experience of our cousins to the south, the United States, where the collapse of dozens and dozens of savings and loan enterprises has cost the American treasury and the American people close to $320 billion U.S., we still have a philosophy that says that we can let these financial institutions police themselves. I am sceptical and my party is sceptical.

I put these points forward in all seriousness, despite some of the interplay which has taken place from side to side here.
There is also a commitment on the part of the government, in this case, to have ownership rules that will become progressively stricter as the institutions involved become larger.
I think in practice this is going to become extremely difficult to put into effect. We will find that as an institution grows it is not going to find it easy to suddenly reduce its ownership level from say 30 per cent down to 10 per cent and so the regulators will be asked to give exceptions and those exceptions will be extremely difficult to accept.
The likely results of this set of bills in front of us are first, a much more concentrated set of financial institutions in this country, much more concentration at the top of the financial system.
Second, we have failed to deal with the question of appropriate control of foreign banks like the Bank of Credit and Commerce which did not follow some of Canada's rules.
Third, we are going to see ourselves with institutions much more vulnerable, I believe, to collapse, as we have experienced in the case of banks and trust companies and as I believe we will experience more in the future.
Finally, I think we are going to see that with the emphasis on self-policing there will be too little supervision of these financial institutions. The financial institutions of any country are crucial, not just in the general economic progress of the country, but in the development, in taking us effectively into new areas of growth and new areas of change. That is why we need good financial institution legislation.
I am pleased with some of the advances in this legislation, but certainly my party and I are unhappy that there are areas such as those I have been mentioning that have not been tackled. This was the chance to meet the challenge of tackling those problems. What we have is compromised legislation in front of us which responds to the larger voices of those who represent our financial institutions instead of responding to the logic of economic development in our country.

subtopic: ACT OF INCORPORATION OF METROPOLITAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY
ACT OF INCORPORATION OF METROPOLITAN GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
that Bill S-6, an act to amend the act of incorporation of Metropolitan General Insurance Company in order to authorize its continuance under the laws of the province of Quebec, be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee H.
He said: Madam Speaker, Metropolitan General Insurance Company was incorporated under chapter 51 of the Statutes of Canada of 1956, and it is governed by the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act.
In April 1987, Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, a major mutual life insurance company whose Canadian head office is located right here in Ottawa, acquired Metropolitan General Insurance Company.
Metropolitan General Insurance Company is a direct underwriter of automobile and home insurance whose agents deal directly with customers without going through independent brokers. The premiums collected by that company all come from Quebec.
In 1990, the total value of the premiums collected by Metropolitan General Insurance Company was $12.2 million, and the company had 26,281 policies in effect.
Following net losses of over $5 million in 1989 and
1990,	the parent company of Metropolitan General Insurance Company announced in January 1991 that this subsidiary would cease operations at the end of March
1991,	unless it found a taker.
On June 4, 1991, the Commerce Group Insurance Company of Saint-Hyacinthe, in your riding, Madam Speaker, which is an insurance company incorporated under federal statutes and one of the two corporations in Commasur Inc., the leader in the field of fire and casualty insurance in Quebec, acquired Metropolitan General Insurance Company. After the takeover, and in order to strengthen the financial situation of Metropolitan General Insurance Company, the Commerce Group Insurance Company bought $9 million of capital stock in Metropolitan General Insurance Company, whose capital and surplus thereby more than tripled.
The Commerce Group Insurance Company does business exclusively through insurance brokers, while Belair Insurance Company, another member of the Commassur Inc. group, like Metropolitan General Insurance Company, deals directly with customers without the intervention of insurance brokers. Belair Insurance Company is incorporated under the Quebec Insurance Act.
Metropolitan General Insurance Company, a direct writer of insurance, wants to continue under the laws of Quebec in order to merge with Belair Insurance Company, also a direct writer of insurance.
The management of Metropolitan General Insurance Company believes that it can offer more competitive products and improve services to policyholders by merging with Belair Insurance Company, a company well-known and well respected among the insurance-buying public in Quebec. With its computer system and its distribution network of 35 sales offices, Belair Insurance Company will absorb an increase of its premium volume at low marginal cost. The synergistic effect of the merger should bring a positive contribution to the Commassur Inc. group's profitability over the next few years. As well, the acquisition of Metropolitan General Insurance Company by Commerce Group Insurance Company Inc. and its merger with Belair Insurance Company will ensure that more than 40 jobs, which would have been lost had the company discontinued operations, will be saved.
In order to be continued under the laws of Quebec, Metropolitan General Insurance Company must be authorized to do so under its basic legislation, and this can only be done through a private bill before the Parliament of Canada. At a special general meeting of shareholders held on November 5, 1991, the continuation of Metropolitan General Insurance Company under the laws of Quebec was unanimously approved.
The proposed transfer of jurisdiction of Metropolitan General Insurance Company is clearly beneficial to its shareholders, customers, and the general public.

In concluding, perhaps I may say that the Commerce Group Insurance Company is located in Saint-Hya-cinthe, in the riding of Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot, and that I sponsored this bill at your request. I want to thank hon. members for their co-operation, because they agreed to a number of exceptional measures that would allow this bill to be adopted today.

Madam Speaker, it is really with great pleasure that we are able to support this bill mainly because earlier today I had talked in this House on the subject of financial institutions and how there is a problem of harmonizing between the federal and provincial regulations. When you have a company trying to meet the requirements of the federal statutes and regulations and trying to meet the requirements of provincial statutes and regulations, you get a kind of jungle where there is really no clear way to go. I look at the 40 jobs that this bill will save that would otherwise be lost.
I also look at what we call in Quebec gros bon sens. This is a bill of what I consider to be gros bon sens. As a Quebecer and as a consumer advocate and a member of Parliament for Chambly, Quebec I am proud to speak on it today. I think we speak with one mind on the necessity of this bill and also the urgency with which we need to get this bill adopted and passed through this House. Therefore I just wish to tell you, Madam Speaker, and perhaps the people who are watching us today as they do many days that many times this House can do something extraordinary. They can speak with one voice on legislation which it considers urgent and necessary.
I would like to conclude with that.
